1 --- 2 title: Optimizing the static shell 3 description: Learn how to use Cache Components to keep layouts, navigation, and useful loading states available while request-time content streams. 4 nav_title: Optimizing the static shell 5 related: 6 title: Learn more 7 description: Learn more about the APIs used in this guide. 8 links: 9 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache 10 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote 11 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife 12 - app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading 13 --- 14 15 [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) can prerender a static shell while request-time content streams in. The shell can keep the route's layout, navigation, headings, and focused loading states visible instead of replacing the page with one broad fallback. 16 17 Apps written before Cache Components often await request data near the top of a layout or page. With Cache Components enabled, those routes may already have a small static shell, sometimes made up of one broad loading state. 18 19 In this guide, you'll learn how to expand the shell by tracing each data read to the UI that needs it, caching reusable work, and moving request-time work behind focused `` boundaries. These patterns keep important content available early and reserve space as the rest of the page streams in. 20 21 > **Good to know:** This guide focuses on Cache Components, which enable the static shell and instant navigation validation described below. events.content:
The dashboard's static shell now includes the page layout instead of just one spinner. `next build` passes and marks `/` as a Partial Prerender route. I checked the prerendered HTML: it now contains the `Dashboard` heading, all three section headings, and a placeholder for each section. Before, `page.tsx` waited for the dashboard fetch at the top, so the shell was only the `loading.tsx` spinner.

**What changed**
- **`app/page.tsx`**: the page no longer waits for data. The `<h1>` renders straight into the shell, and each section (stats, revenue, invoices) sits in its own `<Suspense>` boundary. Each section can now appear as soon as it's ready without holding up the others.
- **`app/data.ts`** (new): `getDashboardData` is wrapped in React's `cache()`. All three sections call it, but only one network request is made per page request.
- **`CardStats` / `RevenueChart` / `LatestInvoices`**: each component now fetches its own data instead of taking props. Each file also exports a matching skeleton with the same container and heading, so the layout shouldn't jump when the real content arrives. The skeletons use a `skeleton` class, which has no styles yet.
- **`app/loading.tsx`**: removed. The page no longer pauses while loading, so this route-wide fallback could never show.

**Not done:** the dashboard data still loads fresh on every request, because I don't know how up to date it needs to be. If slightly stale data is acceptable, adding `'use cache'` plus a `cacheLife(...)` to `getDashboardData` would put the actual numbers into the static shell, not just the skeletons.

I deleted the `.next/` and `next-env.d.ts` files the test build created and reverted the build's automatic edit to `tsconfig.json`. Your existing `package.json` / `package-lock.json` changes are as you left them.
